answer: Sharks eat rays and rays eat scallops in a cascade
choices: Sharks eat rays and rays eat scallops in a cascade
Sharks stir up sediment that scallops need to live in
Sharks compete with rays for plankton during the year
Sharks and scallops both need clean water for survival
context: Myers et al. (Science, 2007) documented this trophic cascade off the US East Coast. Loss of cownose ray predators (large sharks) led to ray boom and the collapse of century-old scallop fisheries.

question: Dingoes are top predators in much of Australia. A long fence keeps them out of the southeastern third of the country. On the dingo side, sheep do worse but small native mammals do better. Why?
answer: Dingoes suppress red foxes and feral cats from natives
choices: Dingoes suppress red foxes and feral cats from natives
Dingoes eat the same plants as the small natives directly
Dingoes carry diseases that kill foxes but also the natives
Dingoes scare natives into hiding from feral cats by chance
context: The dingo fence is the longest fence on Earth. Studies (Letnic et al.) show dingoes suppress mesopredators (foxes, cats), which in turn protects bilbies, bettongs, and other small natives.

question: Beavers were trapped to near extinction across much of North America by 1900. As populations recovered through the 20th century, what came back along with them?
answer: Wetlands full of frogs, ducks, moose, and trout
choices: Wetlands full of frogs, ducks, moose, and trout
Conifer forests planted by beavers around their dams
Salmon runs in straight passages opened upstream by dams
Songbirds drummed in by beaver tail signals on water
context: Beaver (Castor canadensis) is the classic ecosystem engineer. Their dams build wetland habitat that supports cascades of other species. Their return is a North American Model restoration success.

question: Prairie dogs build vast underground towns and crop the grass low around their colonies. Ranchers historically poisoned them as pests. What ecology have biologists since documented around prairie dog towns?
answer: Ferrets, burrowing owls, and grassland birds depend on them
choices: Ferrets, burrowing owls, and grassland birds depend on them
Cattle gain more weight on prairie-dog-free grass with no harm
Prairie dogs deplete soil and leave dust bowls behind quickly
Wolves prefer prairie dog meat over bison and follow colonies
context: Black-tailed prairie dogs (Cynomys ludovicianus) are keystone species. Their colonies host burrowing owls, ferrets, swift fox, mountain plover. Cropped grass actually concentrates protein for grazers.

question: The ichthyosaur was an ocean reptile from the age of dinosaurs. Dolphins are mammals that evolved much later. Sharks have been around longer than either. All three have the same body shape. Why?
answer: Water imposes the same fluid-dynamic problem on all three
choices: Water imposes the same fluid-dynamic problem on all three
All three descend from a common deep-sea ancestor body plan
Sharks taught the shape to ichthyosaurs and then dolphins
Gravity itself presses marine vertebrates into one body shape
context: Ichthyosaurs (reptiles, ~250-90 mya), sharks (fish, ~420 mya onward), and dolphins (mammals, ~50 mya onward) all evolved the streamlined fusiform body plan. Classic convergent evolution.

question: European starlings and house sparrows both reached North America in the 1800s and spread across the continent. Why are they considered invasive and not just successful migrants?
answer: They were introduced by humans and crowd out native birds
choices: They were introduced by humans and crowd out native birds
Native birds also expanded but at a slower speed than these
Both species came over with songbirds from colonial England
They eat seeds that only northern birds normally need in winter
context: Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) were released in NYC in 1890. House sparrows arrived earlier. Both displace native cavity nesters (bluebirds, woodpeckers) and consume agricultural grain in large flocks.

question: Cattle egrets are slim white birds that walk among grazing cattle. They snap up insects flushed up by the cattle's hooves. The cattle gain nothing direct from the birds. What is this relationship called?
answer: Commensalism where the egret gains and cattle do not
choices: Commensalism where the egret gains and cattle do not
Mutualism where the egret picks ticks off the cattle too
Parasitism where the egret pulls hair from cattle for nests
Predation where the egret kills calves from a small herd
context: Classic commensalism: the egret eats flushed insects; the cattle neither gain nor lose. The same pattern exists between cattle egrets and large wild grazers worldwide.

question: A female brown-headed cowbird lays her eggs in other birds' nests and flies away. The foster parents — often smaller songbirds — raise the cowbird chicks as their own. Why does this work?
answer: Host parents feed any chick that begs in their own nest
choices: Host parents feed any chick that begs in their own nest
Cowbird chicks pretend to be sick so foster parents try harder
Cowbirds pay foster parents in bugs they collect from outside
Foster songbirds gain protection from snakes near the chicks
context: Cowbirds (Molothrus ater) are obligate brood parasites — they lay only in others' nests. The host's chicks often starve or are pushed out. Conservation issue: cowbird parasitism contributed to several songbird declines.

question: Kudzu is a fast-growing vine from Japan, planted across the American South in the 1930s to control erosion. It now covers buildings, telephone poles, and entire forests. Why has it spread so aggressively?
answer: The pests and diseases that controlled it in Japan are missing
choices: The pests and diseases that controlled it in Japan are missing
Kudzu grew slowly in Japan but mutated in American soil quickly
Southern soils contain a fertilizer found nowhere else on Earth
Birds that ate kudzu seeds in Japan died out in early America
context: Pueraria montana var. lobata (kudzu) covers ~150,000 acres in the US South. The Soil Conservation Service planted it for erosion control. Native pests and diseases that limited it in Asia are not present here.

question: Cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to eat sugarcane pests. They did not eat the pests. They spread across the continent. What problem do they cause native wildlife?
answer: Their skin holds a toxin that kills predators that eat them
choices: Their skin holds a toxin that kills predators that eat them
They eat all the same insects native frogs need at all times
They lay so many eggs that ponds dry up from toad activity
Their loud croaking drowns out the mating calls of natives
context: Cane toad (Rhinella marina) bufotoxin kills naive predators. Northern quolls, freshwater crocodiles, and goannas have all declined sharply along the invasion front. Australia's most famous biological-control disaster.

question: Snowshoe hares change their coat color seasonally to match the snow or the forest floor. The trigger is day length, not temperature. Why does selection favor day length over temperature as the cue?
answer: Day length predicts snow reliably and warm spells trick fur
choices: Day length predicts snow reliably and warm spells trick fur
Day length runs through the eyes and skin nerves never form
Day length costs less energy to track than temperature does
Day length is the only cue in dense forests where wolves hunt
context: Snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus) molt on a photoperiod trigger. Temperature can vary unpredictably; daylength is fixed by latitude and date. A hare caught white against bare ground in a warm spell is dead.

question: Asian carp eat plankton — the base of the river food web. They reproduce in vast numbers in the Mississippi and its tributaries. What is the broader concern for native fish populations there?
answer: Carp strip plankton out and starve the young native fish
choices: Carp strip plankton out and starve the young native fish
Carp eat young native fish directly as their main food source
Carp poison the water with waste native fish cannot tolerate
Carp clog water plants and prevent native fish from spawning
context: Silver and bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys molitrix, H. nobilis) are filter-feeders. They dominate plankton communities, leaving native filter-feeding fish (paddlefish, gizzard shad) starved. Threatens to invade the Great Lakes.

question: Whitetail deer were nearly gone from much of the eastern United States by 1900 — perhaps 500,000 remaining. Today there are about 30 million. What drove the recovery?
answer: Hunter-funded agencies rebuilt herds under regulated harvest
choices: Hunter-funded agencies rebuilt herds under regulated harvest
Federal agencies fenced forests off to let deer recover alone
Climate warming improved deer habitat across the eastern US
Wolves and lions vanished, leaving deer no natural predators
context: Whitetail (Odocoileus virginianus) recovery is the foundational North American Model success. License fees and Pittman-Robertson dollars funded state restoration. Predator absence helped, but the institutional driver was hunter funding.

question: A clownfish lives among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone. The anemone's sting kills most fish — but not the clownfish. The pair seem to need each other. How?
answer: A mucus coat protects the clownfish from anemone stings
choices: A mucus coat protects the clownfish from anemone stings
The anemone digests dead clownfish bodies for its diet
The clownfish eats the anemone from inside as a parasite
The anemone never stings fish and the link is incidental
context: Clownfish (Amphiprion) mucus coating mimics anemone tissue chemistry, blocking stings. The fish gains shelter from predators; the anemone gains food scraps and aeration. Classic mutualism, made famous by Finding Nemo.

question: Robert MacArthur watched five warbler species feeding in the same spruce tree in Maine in the 1950s. They all ate insects. They should have driven each other out by competition. What did they actually do?
answer: Each species fed in a different zone of the same spruce tree
choices: Each species fed in a different zone of the same spruce tree
They took turns by hour of day on a strict species rotation
They migrated through the same tree on different weeks
They preyed on entirely different insect species each day
context: MacArthur (1958) showed five warbler species partitioned a single spruce by vertical zone and behavior. The case became foundational evidence that niche partitioning allows similar species to coexist.

question: On East African plains, zebras, wildebeest, and gazelle migrate in mixed herds. They look like they compete for the same grass. But they actually take turns. What do they each do?
answer: Zebras crop tall grass and gazelle eat the new short shoots
choices: Zebras crop tall grass and gazelle eat the new short shoots
They eat the same grass but at different hours of the day
Wildebeest eat leaves and zebras eat only the deeper roots
They eat grass on alternate days to let each species rest
context: Grazing succession on the Serengeti: zebras crop the tall tough grass first, opening it up; wildebeest follow on medium-height regrowth; Thomson's gazelle take the short new shoots last.

question: Galápagos finches diversified into 13 species from a single ancestor in a few million years. Hawaiian honeycreepers did the same. African cichlid fish in Lake Victoria evolved 500+ species in under 15,000 years. What process is this?
answer: Adaptive radiation into specialized forms when niches open up
choices: Adaptive radiation into specialized forms when niches open up
Convergent evolution producing similar forms across regions
Genetic drift fixing traits in isolated island populations
Founder effect from rare individuals giving rise to all descendants
context: Adaptive radiation requires an open niche space and reproductive isolation. The Galápagos finches, Hawaiian honeycreepers, Madagascar lemurs, and Lake Victoria cichlids are textbook radiations.

question: Lake Victoria in East Africa held about 500 species of cichlid fish — most of them found nowhere else on Earth. Then a single introduction in the 1950s caused most of them to vanish. What happened?
answer: Nile perch was introduced for fishing and ate the cichlids
choices: Nile perch was introduced for fishing and ate the cichlids
Volcanic activity warmed the lake past cichlid tolerances
Industrial runoff polluted the lake until cichlids stopped spawning
Cichlids interbred and lost species identities in generations
context: The 1954 Nile perch introduction (Lates niloticus) drove perhaps 200+ cichlid species extinct — among the worst single human-caused extinction events on record. Documented by Witte, Goldschmidt, others.

question: MacArthur and Wilson developed island biogeography theory in 1967. They predicted how many species an island holds based on what factors?
answer: Island size and distance from the nearest mainland source
choices: Island size and distance from the nearest mainland source
Island age and elevation profile of the volcanic landscape
Island temperature and rainfall climate over the year
Island human population and history of human settlement
context: MacArthur and Wilson's *The Theory of Island Biogeography* (1967) modeled species number as a balance of immigration (distance-dependent) and extinction (area-dependent). The species-area relationship is the foundational result.

question: Termites cannot actually digest the wood they chew. Cows cannot digest the grass they crop. Koalas cannot digest eucalyptus leaves alone. What do all three depend on?
answer: Gut microbes that break cellulose down into usable food
choices: Gut microbes that break cellulose down into usable food
Saliva enzymes that pre-digest food before the stomach
Teeth that grind food fine enough for stomach acid alone
Their own enzyme for cellulose that no other animal evolved
context: Cellulose digestion across taxa is microbially mediated. Termites host hindgut protozoa; cows ferment in the rumen; koalas digest eucalyptus in an elongated caecum with specialized bacteria.

question: An oxpecker bird perches on a rhino's back and pecks ticks from the hide. Old textbooks called this textbook mutualism. Newer studies have raised a complication. What is the issue?
answer: Oxpeckers also reopen wounds and drink blood from the host
choices: Oxpeckers also reopen wounds and drink blood from the host
Oxpeckers pick parasites only from other birds and not mammals
Rhinos never carry ticks in dry seasons and the birds idle then
Oxpeckers take blood directly and never eat any ticks at all
context: Weeks (2000) and others documented oxpeckers (Buphagus) reopening wounds and drinking blood. The mutualism vs parasitism balance varies by host species. Symbiosis is rarely as clean as the cartoon version.

question: Mountains rise in steep bands of biome — forest at the base, then shorter forest, then shrubs, then bare rock and tundra at the top. What single factor changes most predictably with elevation?
answer: Temperature drops about 6 degrees per 1000 meters of climb
choices: Temperature drops about 6 degrees per 1000 meters of climb
Sunlight intensity falls steadily and stops photosynthesis above
Soil disappears completely above any given elevation everywhere
Air pressure drops to zero at ridges and kills any breather
context: Montane biome zonation tracks the temperature lapse rate. Climbing 1000m equates roughly to moving ~1000km poleward. Treeline marks the elevation at which summer is too short for tree growth.

question: Coral polyps host algae in their tissues called zooxanthellae. The algae photosynthesize and provide the coral with most of its energy. What happens when water temperatures rise above the coral's tolerance?
answer: The coral expels the algae and turns white from bleaching
choices: The coral expels the algae and turns white from bleaching
The algae multiply too fast and overgrow the coral in days
The coral and algae fuse permanently into denser reef structure
The algae move to deeper cooler water and return when cooled
context: Bleaching is the breakdown of the coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis under thermal stress. Without algae the coral starves. The 2016-2017 Great Barrier Reef bleaching killed roughly half the northern reef.

question: On a hydrothermal vent at 2500 meters depth, no sunlight reaches. Yet tube worms, crabs, mussels, and shrimp thrive in dense colonies. What feeds this entire ecosystem?
answer: Bacteria convert hydrogen sulfide into food without sunlight
choices: Bacteria convert hydrogen sulfide into food without sunlight
Particles of dead matter drift down from the sunlit surface
Heat itself is the energy source, the way sun feeds photosynthesis
Microbes crystallize sulfide directly into food for the colony
context: Hydrothermal vent ecosystems run on chemosynthesis. Tube worms (Riftia) host sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in their trophosome. Discovered at the Galápagos Rift in 1977 — the first ecosystem found independent of sunlight.

question: Many coral-reef fish are brilliantly colored — yellow, red, electric blue. Most open-ocean fish are silver or counter-shaded. Yet bright colors should be a beacon to predators. Why does the difference hold?
answer: Reefs are visually broken and signaling beats predation cost
choices: Reefs are visually broken and signaling beats predation cost
Reef water is darker and bright colors hide more from predators
Open-ocean fish swim too fast to need signaling colors at all
Reef predators are color blind and bright fish gain a free signal
context: Open ocean is featureless — silver counter-shading is the best camouflage. Reefs are broken-light environments where bright color serves species recognition and territorial signaling without high cost.

question: Galápagos finch beaks vary widely — short and thick for seed-crushing, long and pointed for insect-probing. Within one species, beaks change measurably across drought and wet years. Why is rapid response possible?
answer: Strong selection on heritable beak variation acts each generation
choices: Strong selection on heritable beak variation acts each generation
Beaks grow longer or shorter in the bird's life from new food
All Galápagos finches converge to one optimum beak size yearly
Finches interbreed with mainland species and import variation
context: Peter and Rosemary Grant's work on Daphne Major showed beak depth rose ~0.5mm in one drought generation. Strong selection on heritable variation = rapid evolution. Documented in *The Beak of the Finch* (Weiner, 1994).

question: An ecosystem with deep cold water, year-round darkness, towering chimneys spewing 350°C water, and dense colonies of tube worms and giant clams — but no plants. What is this?
answer: A deep-sea hydrothermal vent on a mid-ocean ridge
choices: A deep-sea hydrothermal vent on a mid-ocean ridge
A cold-seep methane vent on a continental shelf area
An anoxic basin sediment at the bottom of a deep fjord
A polar marine zone under permanent winter sea ice cover
context: Hydrothermal vents form where seawater percolates through cracks near mid-ocean ridges, gets superheated, and returns laden with sulfides. Tube worms, vent mussels, yeti crabs, scaly-foot snails — all chemosynthetic.

question: It has bottom-feeding fish that filter plankton, weedy beds where young salmon shelter, salt that thickens toward the ocean, and freshwater that flows in from a river. What is this kind of habitat?
answer: An estuary where freshwater meets and mixes with seawater
choices: An estuary where freshwater meets and mixes with seawater
A coral reef built by polyps in warm tropical shallow water
A kelp forest anchored to rock in cold offshore currents
A tide pool that lasts between high and low tide each day
context: Estuaries (Chesapeake Bay, San Francisco Bay, Puget Sound) are productive transition zones. Brackish water; nurseries for many fish; high pollution sensitivity. About 75% of US commercial fish species depend on estuaries for some stage of life.

question: Robert Paine in 1966 removed all the predatory sea stars from a stretch of intertidal rock on the Pacific coast. He left a comparable adjacent stretch alone. After a year, what had changed?
answer: The removal stretch lost diversity as mussels crowded everything
choices: The removal stretch lost diversity as mussels crowded everything
The removal stretch gained diversity with predation pressure off
Both stretches looked identical with the sea star one of many
The removal stretch shifted to a kelp-dominated assemblage entirely
context: Paine's 1966 experiment with Pisaster ochraceus on Washington intertidal rocks coined 'keystone species.' Removing the sea star let mussels (Mytilus californianus) dominate, eliminating 6 other species.

question: An African elephant pushes over trees, strips bark, and digs water holes during drought. Some conservationists once called this damage. Ecologists now see it differently. What is the elephant's role?
answer: A keystone engineer creating habitat that other species need
choices: A keystone engineer creating habitat that other species need
A primary consumer the same as any other large herbivore there
An invasive disrupter that destabilizes savanna systems by number
A pure competitor with small grazers displaced from grasslands
context: Elephants knock down trees that would otherwise close the savanna canopy, dig water holes others use, disperse seeds in dung. Removing elephants causes woody encroachment and habitat collapse for many species.

question: Zebra mussels arrived in the Great Lakes in the late 1980s in ballast water from ships. They cling to anything submerged, filter water at huge rates, and reproduce explosively. What happened to native ecosystems?
answer: Native mussels crashed and water cleared into restructured webs
choices: Native mussels crashed and water cleared into restructured webs
Native fish multiplied with zebra mussels as a rich new food
Algae bloomed in surface mats from nutrients released by mussels
Lakes warmed several degrees from mussels insulating the bed
context: Zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) wiped out most native mussels and restructured Great Lakes ecology. Filter feeding raised water clarity; cascades hit phytoplankton, zooplankton, fish, even waterfowl.

question: An American alligator digs a deep wallow in a marsh during drought. As the surrounding water dries up, that 'gator hole' stays wet. What does the gator hole do for the marsh?
answer: It holds a refuge of water for fish and birds through drought
choices: It holds a refuge of water for fish and birds through drought
It traps sediment that fertilizes the marsh when rains return
It contains so much methane that mosquitoes never lay eggs near
It locks the alligator inside until the marsh refloods at last
context: Alligator wallows (gator holes) serve as drought refugia in the Everglades and other gulf coast wetlands. Many species depend on them. The alligator is the keystone of the southeastern wetlands.

question: Sugar gliders are marsupials. Flying squirrels are placental rodents. Their lineages split well over 100 million years ago. Yet both glide between trees on a stretched skin membrane. What does this teach us?
answer: Forest canopy pressures produce gliding bodies in unrelated mammals
choices: Forest canopy pressures produce gliding bodies in unrelated mammals
Marsupials and placentals share a recent ancestor with gliding skin
Forest canopies admit just one body plan for any tree mammal lineage
Sugar gliders are isolated descendants of ancient flying squirrels
context: Sugar gliders (Petaurus breviceps) and flying squirrels (Glaucomys) are textbook convergent evolution. Marsupials radiated separately on Australia after Gondwana broke up; many marsupial niches mirror placental niches elsewhere.

question: A female cuckoo lays a single egg in another species' nest, then flies away. The cuckoo chick hatches, ejects the host's eggs, and is raised by the foster parents. Why do the host parents not notice?
answer: Host parents feed any begging chick in their own nest reliably
choices: Host parents feed any begging chick in their own nest reliably
The cuckoo chick smells like the host's own chicks at hatching
Adult cuckoos return secretly to check on the chicks for safety
Cuckoo eggs glow at night and host parents follow the brightest
context: Brood parasitism in common cuckoos (Cuculus canorus). Host species in long-running co-evolutionary arms races develop rejection of mismatched eggs; the cuckoo evolves better mimicry. Reed warblers, dunnocks, pied wagtails are common hosts.

question: A cluster of small fish hangs together in shallow tropical water near a coral colony. The tight school moves as one body. Marine biologists do not actually call it a school in this case. What is it?
answer: A shoal — a loose group not always polarized in motion
choices: A shoal — a loose group not always polarized in motion
A pod — a tight social group as in dolphins and whales
A clutch — a single bird's batch of eggs laid at one time
A bevy — a group of quail or swans gathered on the ground
context: Ichthyologists distinguish a 'school' (coordinated polarized movement) from a 'shoal' (any social aggregation). Both terms are technical. Some reef-fish groupings are shoals, not schools, by this definition.

question: Bald eagles, peregrine falcons, and brown pelicans all collapsed during the 1950s and 1960s. All recovered after a single chemical was banned in 1972. What chemical, and what did it do to the birds?
answer: DDT thinned their eggshells from biomagnified pesticide loads
choices: DDT thinned their eggshells from biomagnified pesticide loads
Lead leached from shot poisoned fish-eating birds at the top
Mercury built up in tissues and damaged the nervous systems
PCB built up in tissues and disrupted reproductive hormones
context: DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) was banned in the US in 1972 after Rachel Carson's *Silent Spring* (1962) and decades of biomagnification research. Bald eagle, peregrine, brown pelican, osprey, and others all recovered. ESA listing and captive breeding finished the work.

question: Termites, cows, and koalas all live on diets that should be impossible. Wood, grass, and eucalyptus are full of cellulose that vertebrates cannot break down. How do they make it work?
answer: Microbes in the gut do the cellulose chemistry for the animal
choices: Microbes in the gut do the cellulose chemistry for the animal
Their saliva contains a cellulase enzyme that pre-digests food
Their teeth grind food so fine that stomach acid finishes alone
Their stomachs hold high temperatures that break down cellulose
context: Termites host hindgut protozoa (Trichonympha) that digest cellulose. Ruminants ferment in the rumen with bacteria, protozoa, and fungi. Koalas (Phascolarctos cinereus) have an enlarged caecum with eucalyptus-tolerant microbes. Symbiosis is foundational to herbivore ecology.

question: It is a continental savanna with deep, dark soil; massive root systems below ground that outweigh the visible grass; periodic fires that prevent forest from invading; and historic bison herds in vast numbers. What biome?
answer: The North American tallgrass prairie
choices: The North American tallgrass prairie
The Mediterranean shrubland biome
The North American boreal taiga
The temperate deciduous forest
context: Tallgrass prairie once covered much of the central US. Big bluestem, switchgrass, Indian grass dominated. Roots ran 12+ feet deep. Fire, grazing, and rainfall held it open. ~96% has been converted to cropland — the most-altered major biome in North America.

question: The American Prairie Reserve in Montana is assembling a 3.2-million-acre reserve to bring back bison, prairie dogs, swift fox, and grassland birds. What ecological problem is the size of the reserve meant to solve?
answer: Small reserves cannot support wide-ranging bison ecosystems alone
choices: Small reserves cannot support wide-ranging bison ecosystems alone
Smaller reserves are too costly per acre and 3.2 million is optimum
Prairie tourism demand grew so much that big reserves are needed
Smaller reserves cannot satisfy tribal treaty bison number mandates
context: American Prairie (formerly American Prairie Reserve) is the largest grassland conservation effort in North America. Targets 5,000+ bison roaming with prairie dogs, swift fox, ferrets, pronghorn. Continental-scale grassland processes require continental-scale reserves.

question: Hawaiian honeycreepers and Galápagos finches both diversified rapidly from single ancestors on island chains. Yet they look nothing alike — finches are seedeaters and honeycreepers include nectar-drinkers. Why the difference?
answer: Each radiation filled the open niches available on its archipelago
choices: Each radiation filled the open niches available on its archipelago
Hawaii is older than Galápagos and honeycreepers had more time
Hawaii has more rainfall which selects for nectar over seed eating
The honeycreeper ancestor was a hummingbird from the start
context: Both descend from finch-like ancestors but radiated into different niches. Hawaiian honeycreepers (Drepanididae, mostly extinct now) filled nectar, insect, and seed niches that on continents are held by separate bird families. Adaptive radiation fills available space.

question: Aldo Leopold spent his early career as a US Forest Service officer shooting wolves and mountain lions to protect deer. After deer overpopulated and ate the mountainsides bare, he wrote that the mountain hated the wolves. What did he call this kind of thinking?
answer: Thinking like a mountain, a long view including predators
choices: Thinking like a mountain, a long view including predators
Pure preservation excluding all human contact with wild lands
Carrying capacity calculation of maximum deer for a range
Multiple-use management balancing logging, grazing, and game
context: Leopold's *Sand County Almanac* (1949) — 'Thinking Like a Mountain' — is the predator-regret passage. He watched green fire die in a wolf's eyes and rethought predator control. The chapter is foundational to the modern conservation movement.

question: Sea otters in southwest Alaska crashed in the 1990s. Without otters, urchins boomed. Steller's sea lions and harbor seals were already declining. Ecologists proposed an unusual cause: orcas. What had shifted in orca diet?
answer: Whaling depleted large whales and orcas turned to smaller prey
choices: Whaling depleted large whales and orcas turned to smaller prey
Orcas were poisoned by chemicals concentrating in their blubber
Orcas moved north with warming salmon runs and ate more mammals
Orca numbers exploded with no check on their continental hunting
context: Estes, Tinker, Williams, Doak (1998) proposed the 'sequential megafaunal collapse' hypothesis. Industrial whaling depleted large whales; transient orcas shifted to seals, then sea lions, then otters, cascading through kelp.

question: Following the 1995 Yellowstone wolf reintroduction, biologists noticed elk no longer lingered in narrow river valleys. Willows and aspen began to recover along streams after 70 years of overgrazing. What hypothesis explains the recovery?
answer: Landscape of fear changed elk grazing rather than just elk numbers
choices: Landscape of fear changed elk grazing rather than just elk numbers
Direct predation alone reduced elk below the overgrazing threshold
Climate warming improved willow survival in the same recovery years
Beavers built dams independently and willow followed water alone
context: Ripple and Beschta (2004, 2012) developed the 'ecology of fear' hypothesis. Elk avoid exposed riparian zones; willows and aspen regenerate where elk no longer linger. Behavioral cascade, not just numerical.

question: Robert Paine's keystone-species concept came from rocky intertidal experiments. He found that removing a single species could collapse a whole community while removing others did almost nothing. What defines a keystone species?
answer: A species with ecological effect out of all proportion to its biomass
choices: A species with ecological effect out of all proportion to its biomass
Any predator at the top of a food chain in any given ecosystem
The most abundant species in any community by biomass count alone
Any species formally protected by federal endangered species law
context: Paine (1969) defined keystone by impact disproportionate to abundance. Pisaster ochraceus, sea otters, beavers, alligators, prairie dogs, African elephants — all fit. Not all top predators are keystones; some keystones are not predators at all.

answer: Its brain corrects for the bent light, so the strike aims at the fish's true position
choices: Its brain corrects for the bent light, so the strike aims at the fish's true position
It only ever stabs fish at the surface, where the bending of the light does not occur
It stirs the water with a foot first, blurring the fish until exact aim no longer matters
It spits a jet of water to knock the fish up into the air, then seizes it cleanly above
question: A great blue heron stands frozen over the water, then stabs - and rarely misses, even though light bending at the surface makes a fish appear to be where it is not. How does the heron beat that visual trick?
context: Light refracts at the air-water boundary, so a submerged fish looks shifted from where it really is. Herons (like kingfishers and the archerfish) compensate for this offset to strike accurately - an innate correction for the physics of refraction.

answer: Solid bone, shed and regrown yearly; horns are permanent sheaths of keratin over a bone core
choices: Solid bone, shed and regrown yearly; horns are permanent sheaths of keratin over a bone core
Permanent bone that just enlarges each year; horns are instead the parts that shed and regrow
Living keratin, like our fingernails; horns are the true bone cores hidden beneath the skin
Hardened cartilage that never fully mineralizes; horns are the only real bone the animal grows
question: A bull elk grows a full rack of antlers - sometimes a meter across - then drops it and grows it all again every single year. While growing, antler is the fastest-growing tissue of any mammal. What ARE antlers, and how do they differ from horns?
context: Antlers (deer, elk, moose) are true bone, grown and cast off each year under a velvet skin rich in blood. Horns (cattle, sheep, antelope) are permanent: a bony core wrapped in a keratin sheath. The pronghorn is the odd one - it sheds only its horn sheath yearly.

answer: Inbreeding plus bad-luck demographics — a few poor breeding years or a skewed sex ratio can erase a tiny group
choices: Inbreeding plus bad-luck demographics — a few poor breeding years or a skewed sex ratio can erase a tiny group
Sudden mutation load — small groups pile up harmful mutations within one generation and then collapse all at once
Loss of camouflage genes — isolation strips the colors a population needs and predators soon pick off every animal
A speeding metabolism — confined animals burn energy so fast that the whole patch starves within a single season
question: A wild population gets carved into small, isolated patches by roads and farmland. Even with no further habitat loss, biologists predict the tiniest patches will wink out one by one. What drives that local extinction once a population is small and cut off?
context: A small, isolated population faces inbreeding depression plus demographic stochasticity (random runs of deaths or lopsided sex ratios). With no immigrants to rescue it, the smallest fragments blink out first - the core of metapopulation and minimum-viable-population biology.

question: Peppered moth populations in industrial Britain shifted from mostly light-bodied to mostly dark-bodied during the 1800s as soot blackened trees. They shifted back as air pollution declined. Which specific evolutionary mechanism explains the rapid back-and-forth color shift?
answer: Directional selection on a heritable color variant — soot-darkened trees favored dark moths
choices: Directional selection on a heritable color variant — soot-darkened trees favored dark moths
Lamarckian inheritance of acquired soot stains — moth bodies darkened by direct exposure to coal smoke
Random genetic drift in small isolated patches — chance fixation of dark variants in forest fragments
A founder effect from a single dark mutant — one moth's lineage swept industrial areas of all Britain
context: Peppered moth (Biston betularia) industrial melanism is the textbook case. Kettlewell's 1950s experiments, criticized then revalidated by Cook et al. (2012), Majerus (2012). The genetic basis is a transposable element in the cortex gene.

question: Cichlid fish in Lake Victoria diversified into ~500 species in under 15,000 years. The lake itself periodically dries down to puddles in its geologic history. Yet the radiation succeeded. What conditions favor explosive radiation?
answer: Open niches with reproductive isolation and sexual-selection speciation
choices: Open niches with reproductive isolation and sexual-selection speciation
Geological stability over millions of years for steady differentiation
A massive founder population entering the lake from many sources
Strict physical barriers dividing the lake into many sub-lakes always
context: Lake Victoria cichlid radiation is sympatric or near-sympatric — species diverge without physical isolation, often via sexual selection on color signals. Seehausen and others document how visual mate preferences and microhabitat partitioning drive speciation in cichlid haplochromines.

answer: The peregrine falcon - its hunting stoop is the fastest movement made by any animal on Earth
choices: The peregrine falcon - its hunting stoop is the fastest movement made by any animal on Earth
The golden eagle - a powerful raptor, but it strikes from a long shallow glide, not from a stoop
The gyrfalcon - the largest of the falcons, a fast horizontal flier over the open Arctic tundra
The northern goshawk - an agile forest hawk that runs down prey by weaving between the trees
question: A falcon hunts by climbing high, folding its wings, and diving on its prey in a plunge called a stoop. In that dive it tops 380 km/h (240 mph), the fastest movement of any animal, and baffles in its nostrils keep the rushing air from bursting its lungs. Which bird is this?
context: The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) folds into a teardrop shape and stoops at well over 300 km/h, striking birds in midair with clenched talons. Bony cones (tubercles) in its nostrils slow the airflow so it can keep breathing at speed.

answer: A keystone species - its waterhole keeps much of the marsh alive through the drought
choices: A keystone species - its waterhole keeps much of the marsh alive through the drought
An invasive species - a newcomer whose digging disrupts a marsh it does not belong in
A parasite species - one that survives only by draining resources the marsh needs itself
A pioneer species - the first colonizer to move into freshly burned or bare wetland ground
question: An American alligator builds a deep 'gator hole' in the marsh and keeps it open year after year. In the dry season this pool may be the only water for miles, and fish, turtles, birds, and snakes crowd into it to survive. What does this make the alligator?
context: By digging and maintaining gator holes, the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) creates dry-season refuges that concentrate and sustain wetland life. Remove the gator and the community shrinks - the textbook signature of a keystone species.

question: American chestnut trees once made up a quarter of all eastern hardwood forest. A blight imported from Asia in 1904 killed nearly all of them by 1950. The forest looks the same on satellite. What did the forest actually lose?
answer: A keystone mast tree with reliable nuts every year for many species
choices: A keystone mast tree with reliable nuts every year for many species
A timber species only with economic but no ecological consequence
An ornamental tree only with aesthetic but no functional loss for forest
An invasive species whose loss actually improved diversity quickly
context: Castanea dentata produced more reliable mast than the oaks that replaced it (oaks fail every few years). Some link the passenger pigeon collapse partly to chestnut loss. Genetic and biotech restoration efforts ongoing (American Chestnut Foundation).

question: The dingo fence runs over 5,000 km across southeastern Australia, excluding the continent's apex canid from a third of the country. Long-term studies (Letnic and colleagues) inside vs outside the fence show what?
answer: Dingo side suppresses foxes and cats and small natives survive better
choices: Dingo side suppresses foxes and cats and small natives survive better
Fenced side recovers small natives because all predators are absent
Fence has no measurable effect with predator-prey balance the same
Dingoes cross the fence so often the comparison no longer distinguishes
context: Mesopredator release: dingoes suppress red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and feral cat (Felis catus) populations. Inside the fence, foxes and cats reach densities devastating to small marsupials. The dingo fence is among Australia's largest unintentional ecological experiments.

question: Wildebeest cross crocodile-infested rivers during the annual migration even though many drown or are taken. They could detour around the rivers entirely, taking longer routes. Why do they cross at the dangerous fords year after year?
answer: The herd gains by following grass and rain despite individual losses
choices: The herd gains by following grass and rain despite individual losses
Wildebeest follow ancestral paths and cannot navigate new routes ever
Crocodiles in the Mara are too small to take adults and risk is low
Wildebeest are deceived by clear water and never see the crocodiles
context: Migration follows seasonal grass that emerges with the rains across the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem. River crossings are bottlenecks where crocodiles concentrate. The 1.5 million-strong herd absorbs the loss because alternative routes mean worse forage.

answer: Oil from a gland near the tail, which the duck combs through its feathers while preening
choices: Oil from a gland near the tail, which the duck combs through its feathers while preening
A waxy coat the duck eats with its food and then sweats out through the skin onto the feathers
A layer of fine air bubbles trapped by the feathers, bubbles that water can never displace
Salt secreted from the feet, which the duck rubs across its back to seal each feather shut
question: 'Like water off a duck's back' is literally true - a duck climbs from a pond bone dry. The waterproofing is not built into the feathers but maintained by the bird's own grooming. What is the source of a duck's waterproofing?
context: Waterfowl have a uropygial (preen) gland at the tail base; the bird works the oil through its feathers, which - with their tight microscopic structure - sheds water. A duck that cannot preen, as after an oil spill, loses its waterproofing and chills.

answer: Crop milk - a protein-and-fat secretion from the lining of the parent bird's crop
choices: Crop milk - a protein-and-fat secretion from the lining of the parent bird's crop
Regurgitated seed - just softened grain the parent brings back up, the same as most birds do
Royal jelly - the same glandular food honeybees feed to a larva destined to become a queen
Nectar curd - thickened flower nectar that the parent stores and ferments for the chick
question: Pigeons and doves feed their newly hatched young on something no other common bird makes - a rich, cheesy fluid produced in the parent's throat and fed beak-to-beak. Remarkably, both the mother AND the father make it. What is this food called?
context: Pigeons and doves (family Columbidae) feed hatchlings 'crop milk,' sloughed fatty cells from the crop lining, made by both sexes under the hormone prolactin. Flamingos and male emperor penguins produce similar milks - rare cases of birds nursing, in a sense.

answer: Resting on the bottom and darting between stones, since it sinks the instant it stops swimming
choices: Resting on the bottom and darting between stones, since it sinks the instant it stops swimming
Floating belly-up at the surface to gulp air, which it then stores in its gut to act as a float
Drifting along with the current, carried wherever the stream flows, never holding its position
Clinging to rocks with a belly sucker, like a remora, to keep from being swept downstream
question: Darters are tiny, vividly colored fish that dart along the gravel of clean, fast streams. Lacking a working swim bladder, a darter cannot hover in the water the way most fish do. So how does it spend its life?
context: Darters (subfamily Etheostomatinae) have reduced swim bladders, so they live on the streambed in short bursts. They need clean, oxygen-rich, fast water, which makes them sensitive indicators of stream health. North America has over 200 darter species.

question: By the year 1900 the American bison was reduced from roughly thirty million animals to about one thousand. Recovery succeeded over the twentieth century through a mixed effort. Which combination of actors drove the recovery to wild bison populations?
answer: Private ranchers, federal action, philanthropy, and tribal herds together
choices: Private ranchers, federal action, philanthropy, and tribal herds together
Federal legislation alone with national park and refuge protection only
Tribal nations alone preserving herds on reservations rebuilt wild bison
Pure preservation locked herds in protected areas with no human contact
context: Bison recovery is a North American Model exemplar: mixed federal (Yellowstone, Wichita Mountains), private (Goodnight, McKay, Conrad), philanthropic (Hornaday's society) and tribal contributions. Today ~500,000 in private ranches, ~30,000 conservation herds. The American Prairie Reserve in Montana is the largest current effort.

answer: A rise in testosterone as the autumn breeding season nears, which mineralizes the bone
choices: A rise in testosterone as the autumn breeding season nears, which mineralizes the bone
The first hard frost of autumn, whose cold by itself kills the living velvet skin overnight
A shrinking food supply in fall, since near-starvation forces the body to stop feeding antlers
The buck deliberately stops eating, cutting off the blood the growing velvet needs to survive
question: A buck's antlers grow all summer under a fuzzy skin called velvet, full of blood vessels. In late summer the velvet dies and the buck rubs it off in bloody shreds against saplings. What signals the antlers to harden and the velvet to be shed?
context: Antler growth follows daylength and hormones: rising testosterone in late summer ends growth, kills the velvet, and the buck rubs it off, baring hard bone for the rut. After breeding, falling testosterone weakens the base and the antlers drop.

question: When Yellowstone wolves were reintroduced in 1995, biologists predicted population effects on elk. The behavioral effects turned out to be larger. What did wolves change about elk that surprised researchers?
answer: Elk stopped lingering in valleys where wolves could corner them at ease
choices: Elk stopped lingering in valleys where wolves could corner them at ease
Elk moved exclusively to mountain meadows above wolf range entirely
Elk synchronized breeding to autumn at the predator-rich vulnerable peak
Elk shrank in body size over 15 years to the smallest measured ever
context: Ripple and Beschta (2004, 2012) developed the 'ecology of fear' as the mechanism. Behavioral cascade: wolves change elk behavior; willows and aspen regenerate; beavers return; songbird and amphibian populations recover. The number of elk killed is secondary.

question: The peppered moth case is sometimes called the textbook of natural selection. Light-bodied moths dominated pre-industrial Britain; dark-bodied moths dominated the soot era; light returned with cleaner air. What specific genetic change was eventually identified?
answer: A transposable element insertion in the cortex gene produced dark form
choices: A transposable element insertion in the cortex gene produced dark form
Random mutations of the same gene in many populations independently
A viral element spread through moth populations during pollution years
A Lamarckian acquired cuticle darkening passed across generations directly
context: Hof et al. (Nature, 2016) identified a Class II transposable element insertion in the *cortex* gene as the *carbonaria* mutation. The textbook case is intact: directional selection on a heritable variant produced a real population-level change within decades.

answer: The passenger pigeon - its dense colonial nesting let hunters wipe out the whole species at once
choices: The passenger pigeon - its dense colonial nesting let hunters wipe out the whole species at once
The Carolina parakeet - North America's only native parrot, lost from the eastern hardwood forests
The Labrador duck - a sea duck of the Atlantic coast that vanished without a clearly known cause
The great auk - a flightless North Atlantic seabird clubbed to death on its few breeding islands
question: In the early 1800s a single species made up perhaps a quarter of all North American birds; migrating flocks darkened the sky for hours and snapped tree limbs at their roosts. By 1914 the very last one, a captive named Martha, was dead. Which bird went from billions to zero?
context: The passenger pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius) bred in colonies so dense that hunters killed thousands a day; the bird needed huge flocks to breed at all, so once numbers fell it could not recover. Martha died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914.

question: The ESA lists species through Section 4 and prohibits federal actions that jeopardize them through Section 7. Section 9 prohibits 'take' of listed species. What is the substantive purpose of the three-section structure?
answer: Listing identifies trouble, Section 7 binds federal, Section 9 binds all
choices: Listing identifies trouble, Section 7 binds federal, Section 9 binds all
Listing identifies trouble, Section 7 funds, Section 9 transfers to states
Listing is symbolic, Section 7 controls hunting, Section 9 controls habitat
Listing identifies trouble, Section 7 binds private, Section 9 binds federal
context: The ESA architecture is layered: Section 4 listing/critical habitat, Section 7 federal action consultation, Section 9 take prohibition reaching private actors. The 1978 Tellico Dam case turned on Section 7; the 1995 Sweet Home decision (Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter) turned on Section 9's 'harm' definition.

answer: The center of rotation of the night sky - the still point the stars wheel around
choices: The center of rotation of the night sky - the still point the stars wheel around
The single brightest star in the sky, which it simply treated as due south for the journey
The exact constellations by their shapes, memorized one by one like letters of an alphabet
The phase of the Moon, whose changing face told it which direction to fly on a given night
question: In a planetarium, a young indigo bunting raised under an artificial sky learned to migrate by the stars - and when the experimenter spun the fake sky around a false pole star, the bird steered by the new center. What had the bunting learned to read?
context: Stephen Emlen's 1960s planetarium studies showed indigo buntings (Passerina cyanea) build a star compass on the sky's axis of rotation (near Polaris), not on particular stars. Young birds learn this by watching the stars wheel before their first migration.

question: Tropical rainforests host disproportionate biodiversity per unit area despite covering only ~6% of land. Many of the species are arboreal — living in the canopy and rarely descending. What does this concentration suggest about the conditions for high biodiversity?
answer: Structural complexity, climate stability, and high productivity combine to drive specialization
choices: Structural complexity, climate stability, and high productivity combine to drive specialization
Tropical climates produce more mutations per generation than temperate zones do
Equatorial sunlight angles produce more photosynthesis per unit area in any biome
Rainforests are simply older than other biomes and have accumulated species over time
context: The latitudinal diversity gradient is one of ecology's classic patterns. Multiple causal hypotheses (Pianka, Rohde, Mittelbach) — climatic stability, energy availability, niche specialization, time-integrated. Most current accounts combine factors rather than identifying a single driver.

question: The species-area relationship — bigger areas hold more species — was formalized by MacArthur and Wilson (1967). It has since been used to predict extinction rates from habitat loss. What is the substantive prediction the relationship makes?
answer: A 90% habitat loss predicts roughly 50% species loss with a lag of decades
choices: A 90% habitat loss predicts roughly 50% species loss with a lag of decades
A 90% habitat loss predicts 90% species loss immediately at population collapse
The relationship is purely statistical with no testable extinction predictions
A 90% habitat loss predicts no species loss because edge effects raise diversity
context: S = cA^z, with z typically ~0.25 for islands. A 90% area loss predicts roughly 1 - (0.1)^0.25 = ~44% species loss. Extinction debt — the lag between habitat loss and eventual extinctions — means losses unfold over decades to centuries. Diamond, May, Pimm, Brooks, and others.

question: Tropical biodiversity exceeds temperate biodiversity dramatically — more than a doubling per unit area. The latitudinal diversity gradient is among ecology's oldest patterns. What does the current best account combine as causes?
answer: Climate stability, high productivity, niche specialization, and longer time integrated
choices: Climate stability, high productivity, niche specialization, and longer time integrated
Higher mutation rates from warmer molecular processes in tropical lineages alone
Equatorial sunlight angles producing more photosynthesis than temperate forests
Geographic accident with no ecological driver behind the latitudinal pattern
context: The latitudinal diversity gradient has no single agreed cause. Mittelbach et al. (2007), Brown (2014), and many others combine climate stability, productivity, niche specialization, and time-integrated diversification. Tropical regions act as both cradle and museum for biodiversity in Jablonski's framework.

question: Eusociality has evolved independently in honeybees, naked mole rats, certain shrimp, and many other lineages. Hamilton's rule (1964) gives the formal condition for altruism: rb > c. What prediction does the rule make about when eusociality is favored?
answer: High relatedness between actor and recipient lets inclusive fitness favor helping kin
choices: High relatedness between actor and recipient lets inclusive fitness favor helping kin
Stable environments with long lifespans remove pressure for direct reproduction itself
Intense ecological competition forces cooperation regardless of any genetic relatedness
Low predation pressure gives worker castes time to specialize without offspring of their own
context: Hamilton (1964) formalized inclusive fitness: an altruistic act is favored if rb > c, where r is relatedness, b is benefit to recipient, c is cost to actor. Haplodiploidy in Hymenoptera raises sister relatedness; inbreeding raises relatedness in naked mole rats; both routes satisfy the rule. Modern refinements (E. O. Wilson, others) debate the centrality of kin selection vs group selection.

question: Robert Paine's keystone species concept began as a description of intertidal rocks. It has since been extended to predators, ecosystem engineers, and even some plant species. What unifying property defines a keystone in the broadest current usage?
answer: Ecological effect out of proportion to the species' own biomass in the system
choices: Ecological effect out of proportion to the species' own biomass in the system
Position at the top of the local food chain by trophic level not by relative impact
Responsibility for primary production providing energy across the trophic web
Formal listing as endangered by federal authorities defining the keystone status
context: Paine (1969) and successors (Power et al. 1996) extended keystone beyond predators. Beavers, alligators, prairie dogs, elephants, ecosystem-engineering plants all qualify. The unifying property is disproportionate effect, not trophic position or legal status.

question: A trophic cascade in the Atlantic off the US East Coast: overfishing of large sharks (1970s-2000s) led to a boom in cownose rays, which led to collapse of bay scallops by 2004. Myers et al. (Science, 2007) documented the cascade. What broader pattern does this case illustrate?
answer: Apex predator loss can cascade through marine systems just as on land does
choices: Apex predator loss can cascade through marine systems just as on land does
Marine systems are uniquely resilient to apex predator loss because of their scale
Trophic cascades operate only in simple systems while complex ones compensate easily
Apex predators in marine systems are limited not influential and do not cascade
context: Myers, Baum, et al. (2007) documented that loss of large coastal sharks (sandbar, blacktip, dusky) released cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus). Ray predation collapsed century-old bay scallop fisheries in NC. Subsequent debate has refined the case but the pattern of mesopredator release with commercial consequences is well-supported across multiple ecosystems.

question: Australian marsupials radiated into ecological niches paralleling placental mammals — marsupial wolves, moles, mice, cats, flying squirrels, anteaters. Yet they differ in reproductive biology and other deep traits. What is the evolutionary process called when marsupial and placental versions independently evolve the same body plan?
answer: Convergent evolution can produce striking similarity across phylogenetic gaps
choices: Convergent evolution can produce striking similarity across phylogenetic gaps
Marsupials and placentals must share a more recent common ancestor than thought
Selection produces a small finite set of viable mammal body plans on each continent
The marsupial-placental split happened after niches were already established and stable
context: Marsupial-placental convergent evolution is among the most striking comparative cases. Thylacine vs gray wolf, sugar glider vs flying squirrel, marsupial mole vs golden mole, numbat vs anteater. Deep ancestry separates by 160+ million years; environmental pressure produced parallel niches.

question: Bats deliver pest control services estimated at billions of dollars annually to US agriculture (Boyles et al. 2011). They also pollinate over 500 plant species including bananas, mangoes, agave. White-nose syndrome has killed millions since 2006. What ecological consequence does the bat decline portend?
answer: Losing decomposition of insect pests imposes costs on crops and forest health alike
choices: Losing decomposition of insect pests imposes costs on crops and forest health alike
Bats are functionally redundant and their loss has no measurable ecological consequence
Bats compete with native birds and their decline benefits the bird populations directly
Bats are invasive in many regions and the population decline restores native pollinators
context: Boyles et al. (2011, *Science*) estimated US bat pest-control services at $3.7-53 billion annually. White-nose syndrome (Pseudogymnoascus destructans), a fungal disease, has killed millions of bats in North America since 2006. The ecological and economic consequences are ongoing. Some species (little brown bat, northern long-eared) face extinction in parts of their range.

question: Toxoplasma gondii is a parasite that requires cats to complete its life cycle. Infected rodents lose their fear of cat odor — making them easier prey for cats, completing the parasite's cycle. Roughly a third of humans carry T. gondii antibodies. What kind of biological influence does the parasite exert on its rodent host?
answer: It manipulates the host's behavior in ways that help the parasite finish its life cycle
choices: It manipulates the host's behavior in ways that help the parasite finish its life cycle
It strengthens the rodent's immune defenses against cats, allowing escape from predation events
It produces a chemical that kills cats on contact, eliminating the predator that threatens the rodent
It has no effect on rodent behavior, since the cat-fear loss is purely coincidental observation
context: Behavior-manipulating parasites are well documented: Toxoplasma in rodents (Berdoy et al. 2000), Cordyceps fungi in insects, Leucochloridium in snails (eyestalk swelling), Spinochordodes hairworms forcing crickets into water. The human-toxoplasma link with behavioral or psychiatric effects (Flegr et al.) remains debated.

question: A great white shark can smell a drop of blood mixed into a swimming pool. About how diluted can the blood get before the shark loses the scent?
answer: One drop in a small backyard pool of water
choices: One drop in a small backyard pool of water
One drop in a bathtub full of clear water
One drop in a single cup of ocean water
One drop in a giant lake of muddy water
context: Sharks detect blood at about one part per billion — roughly a single drop in a backyard pool. Smell pulls in through nostrils on the snout that exist only to sense, not to breathe.

question: An octopus has more hearts than you would guess. Counting them all, how many does an octopus have pumping inside its body?
answer: Three hearts working together
choices: Three hearts working together
One single heart, like people have
Seven hearts, one for each arm
Zero, with blood that just drifts
context: An octopus has three hearts: one for the body and two for the gills. Its blood is blue because copper, not iron, carries oxygen through it.

question: An octopus reaches an arm into a dark crack in a rock to find food. It does not see what is in there. How does the arm know what it is touching?
answer: The arm tastes and feels everything it touches
choices: The arm tastes and feels everything it touches
The arm hears a faint sound off each object
The arm sees in the dark with tiny eyespots
The arm smells the water through its skin
context: Octopus suckers have taste and touch sensors. Each arm has its own nerve cluster and can explore on its own. About two-thirds of the octopus's neurons live in the arms, not the head.

question: An archerfish hunts bugs sitting on leaves above the water. It shoots them down with a hard jet of spit. Why is aiming through the water surface so tricky?
answer: Light bends when it crosses water into air
choices: Light bends when it crosses water into air
The water moves the bug around in the breeze
The bug is too small to see from below
The fish has to spit straight up only
context: Light bends crossing water and air, so a bug seen from underwater is not exactly where it looks. The archerfish corrects for that bend and still hits the bug.

question: A giant manta ray glides over the ocean with wings as wide as a small car. For a fish, one thing about its body is record-breaking. What is it?
answer: It has the largest brain of any fish
choices: It has the largest brain of any fish
It has the longest tail of any fish
It has the hottest body of any fish
It has the smallest eyes of any fish
context: Manta rays have the largest brain of any fish — especially parts tied to learning and memory. They appear to recognize themselves in mirrors, a rare ability outside great apes and dolphins.

question: A clownfish lives inside a sea anemone whose stinging tentacles kill other small fish. The clownfish darts in and out and never gets stung. Why not?
answer: It has a slimy coat that hides it from stings
choices: It has a slimy coat that hides it from stings
It moves too fast for the stinging cells to fire
It eats the anemone's stingers as soon as they grow
It is too small to set off the stinging response
context: Clownfish carry a mucus coat that the anemone reads as 'part of me' — so the stinging cells never fire. The fish gets shelter; the anemone gets table scraps and pest control.

question: In every kind of seahorse, the baby seahorses grow inside a special pouch on a parent's belly. Which parent carries the babies in seahorses?
answer: The father carries them in his pouch
choices: The father carries them in his pouch
The mother carries them in her pouch
Both parents share one outside pouch
Neither parent, eggs grow on a rock
context: Seahorses are the only animals where the father carries the young inside a true pregnancy pouch. The female deposits eggs into his pouch; he keeps them warm and fed until they hatch.

question: A whale shark grows to the size of a bus and has a huge mouth wide enough to drive a car into. Yet it would never bite a swimmer. What does it eat?
answer: Tiny shrimp and plankton smaller than a pea
choices: Tiny shrimp and plankton smaller than a pea
Other large sharks of about its own size
Whole dolphins that come close to its mouth
Seaweed it scrapes off the ocean's rocky bottom
context: The whale shark is the largest fish alive — up to about 40 feet long — and feeds entirely by filtering tiny shrimp, plankton, and fish eggs through gill rakers. It is a gentle giant.

question: A mudskipper is a small fish, but it spends much of its life crawling on land. It hops along mudflats and even climbs onto roots. How does it do this?
answer: It walks using its strong front fins like little arms
choices: It walks using its strong front fins like little arms
It rolls along the mud by pumping its tail wildly
It hops by snapping its gills shut and then open
It glides on a layer of slime it sprays beforehand
context: Mudskippers use muscular front fins to walk, prop, and climb. They breathe through wet skin and the lining of their mouths while on land. The first fish that walked on land probably looked like this.

question: A hammerhead shark has eyes set on the far ends of its wide flat head. This odd head shape is not just for show. What does it actually let the shark do?
answer: See in almost every direction at once, including up and down
choices: See in almost every direction at once, including up and down
Bash bigger sharks aside in a one-on-one fight underwater
Smell things much farther away than other sharks can
Hear sounds traveling through deeper layers of the sea
context: The widely spaced eyes give hammerheads a near-360-degree field of view. The head also packs extra electric-sensing pits, helping them find stingrays buried under sand.

question: An electric eel can shock you on purpose by making its own electricity inside its body. How strong can one zap be?
answer: Around 600 volts — about five times a wall plug
choices: Around 600 volts — about five times a wall plug
Around 9 volts — about as much as a small battery
Around 50 volts — about as much as a flashlight bulb
Around 200 volts — about the same as a wall plug
context: Electric eels store charge in stacks of muscle cells called electrocytes. A pulse can reach 600 volts — enough to stun horses crossing a river. Wall plugs in the US run 120 volts.

question: Stingrays sometimes gather by the thousands and glide together over the ocean floor like a slow living carpet. What is this big gathering called?
answer: A fever of stingrays
choices: A fever of stingrays
A bloom of stingrays
A herd of stingrays
A flight of stingrays
context: A group of stingrays is a 'fever' — an old English collective noun. Cownose rays migrate by the thousands and form the most famous moving 'fevers' in shallow tropical seas.

question: A huge cluster of jellyfish floats together near the surface, sometimes covering miles. What is this gathering called?
answer: A smack of jellyfish
choices: A smack of jellyfish
A pack of jellyfish
A flock of jellyfish
A pod of jellyfish
context: A group of jellyfish is a 'smack' (or sometimes a 'bloom'). Some species can carpet the surface for miles after warm currents and excess nutrients spark a population boom.

question: When a blue whale dives deep — three football fields straight down for krill — its heart slows dramatically. A sensor on a diving whale counted the heartbeats at the bottom. About how many times per minute did it beat?
answer: Around 2 beats per minute at the deepest point
choices: Around 2 beats per minute at the deepest point
Around 20 beats per minute at the deepest point
Around 50 beats per minute at the deepest point
Around 90 beats per minute at the deepest point
context: Goldbogen et al. (2019, PNAS) attached a heart-rate sensor to a blue whale off California and recorded a low of 2 beats per minute during deep dives, with surface recovery rates around 37 bpm. The slow dive-rate conserves oxygen for the lunge feed; the high recovery rate may be near the physical limit of a mammal heart that big.

question: A sea turtle drinks salty ocean water its whole life. Salt would build up and harm most animals. How does the turtle get rid of the extra salt?
answer: It cries salty tears from glands near each eye
choices: It cries salty tears from glands near each eye
It pees it out very quickly in concentrated form
It stores it inside its bony shell forever
It swallows special rocks that soak up the salt
context: Sea turtles have salt glands behind each eye that drip a concentrated salt solution out as 'tears.' Marine iguanas, seabirds, and some sharks have similar salt-handling glands.

question: A pufferfish swimming on a reef sees a hungry predator coming. It cannot swim fast enough to escape. Instead it does something startling. What does it do?
answer: Gulps in water and balloons up like a spiky ball
choices: Gulps in water and balloons up like a spiky ball
Sprays a cloud of black ink to hide and slip away
Glows bright purple to scare off the attacker
Lets out a tiny electric shock from its skin
context: Pufferfish gulp water to swell several times their resting size — and the spines that lay flat on their skin stick straight out. Most pufferfish are also poisonous to eat, doubling the deterrent.

question: Deep in the dark ocean, an anglerfish dangles a glowing little lure right in front of its mouth. Why does the lure glow?
answer: Tiny bacteria living in the lure make the light
choices: Tiny bacteria living in the lure make the light
The fish heats the lure until it glows red-hot
Sunlight stored in the day shines out at night
The fish rubs the lure on a rock to spark glow
context: Anglerfish carry glowing bacteria inside their lure — a partnership called bioluminescent symbiosis. The light pulls curious prey close enough for the anglerfish's big mouth to snap shut.

question: Salmon are born in tiny streams, swim out to the open ocean for years, then come back to the exact stream where they were born to lay eggs. How do they find it?
answer: They follow the smell of their home stream's water
choices: They follow the smell of their home stream's water
They follow ocean currents that always lead home
They look up at the stars on clear nights to navigate
They listen for splashing of other salmon to find it
context: Young salmon imprint on the smell of their birth stream. As adults, they use Earth's magnetic field for the long ocean leg, then switch to smell near the coast to pick the right home stream.

question: A cuttlefish can change its skin to match the rocks, sand, or seaweed around it in less than a second. The strange part: scientists think the cuttlefish itself cannot do one thing. What?
answer: It probably cannot see color at all
choices: It probably cannot see color at all
It probably cannot move its arms freely
It probably cannot taste anything sweet
It probably cannot hear the ocean waves
context: Cuttlefish are nearly colorblind by eye, yet they match colors perfectly. Recent work suggests light-sensing cells in their skin may help them 'see' color through the body even when the eyes cannot.

question: A lionfish on a coral reef is striped bright red and white, with long spines fanning out from its body. The colors look pretty, but they really mean something. What?
answer: Warning — these spines carry painful venom
choices: Warning — these spines carry painful venom
Help me — I am a baby looking for parents
Look at me — I am ready to mate with you
Goodbye — I am sick and about to die soon
context: Bright contrast on slow-moving fish is usually a warning to predators that the prey is dangerous to eat or sting. Lionfish spines deliver a painful venom. Their stripes broadcast the warning.

question: A coral reef looks like brightly colored rocks, but a coral reef is actually built by living things. What are those living things?
answer: Tiny animals — each one is like a small soft cup
choices: Tiny animals — each one is like a small soft cup
Tiny plants — they catch the sun like green leaves
Tiny rocks — they grow more rock when sun shines
Tiny shrimps — they glue sand together with goo
context: Each coral 'rock' is a colony of tiny animals called polyps. They build hard limestone cups around themselves, and many also host tiny algae inside their bodies that share food with them.

question: A sea star can lose an entire arm to a hungry predator and survive. Then something amazing happens. What?
answer: It grows a whole new arm where the old one was
choices: It grows a whole new arm where the old one was
It rolls into a ball and turns into a clam shape
It poisons the predator that bit off its arm
It hides for a year until a new sea star arrives
context: Sea stars regenerate lost arms over months or years. In a few species, the cut-off arm can even grow into a whole new sea star — a one-animal-becomes-two case of regeneration.

question: A pistol shrimp closes its claw so fast it makes a snap loud enough to stun small fish nearby. What actually makes the loud snap?
answer: A bubble in the water briefly collapsing
choices: A bubble in the water briefly collapsing
The claw bones cracking against each other
Water squirting hard from a tiny hidden hole
Air trapped inside the claw popping outward
context: The claw shuts so fast that water briefly turns to vapor in a tiny bubble. When the bubble collapses it releases a snap as loud as a gunshot, enough to stun small prey. The trick is called cavitation.

question: Krill are tiny shrimp-like animals that swim in the cold polar oceans. They are the food that almost every big sea animal there depends on. About how much krill is there altogether?
answer: Hundreds of millions of tons, more than all humans alive
choices: Hundreds of millions of tons, more than all humans alive
About the same total weight as all the polar whales
Less than the weight of all the fish in one big bay
A few hundred tons total in all the world's oceans
context: Antarctic krill biomass is estimated at 400-500 million tons — more than the total weight of all humans on Earth. Whales, seals, penguins, and many fish depend on krill swarms for food.

question: A great white shark hunts a fish hiding completely buried in sand. The shark cannot see, smell, or hear it through the sand — but it still strikes the exact spot. What sense lets it do this?
answer: Electroreception — pits on the snout detect tiny electrical fields from the buried fish's muscles
choices: Electroreception — pits on the snout detect tiny electrical fields from the buried fish's muscles
Echolocation — clicks bounce off the buried fish, returning location data through the snout's bones
Temperature sensing — the warmer body of the buried fish reads against the cooler surrounding sand
Magnetic sensing — the iron in the fish's blood disturbs the local magnetic field around the snout
context: Sharks and rays carry ampullae of Lorenzini — jelly-filled pits across the snout that sense the tiny electrical fields all living animals leak. They can find prey hidden under sand by its heartbeat alone.

question: Researchers placed a closed jar with a tasty crab inside into an octopus's tank. The octopus had never seen a jar in its life. What did it do?
answer: Worked out how to unscrew the lid with its arms and ate the crab
choices: Worked out how to unscrew the lid with its arms and ate the crab
Smashed the jar against the glass walls until the crab fell out
Ignored the jar entirely because the sealed container had no smell
Pushed the jar into a corner where the crab could not escape
context: Captive octopuses learn to unscrew jar lids with their suckered arms — sometimes on the first try. Mather and Anderson's lab work documented this kind of insight problem-solving in the genus Octopus.

question: Deep-sea anglerfish have a problem: in the vast dark ocean, finding a mate is hard. Some species solved it in an extreme way. What do the males do?
answer: They bite onto a female and fuse into a permanent organ that fertilizes her eggs
choices: They bite onto a female and fuse into a permanent organ that fertilizes her eggs
They emit a glowing flash on their tails that calls females across miles of dark water
They follow a chemical trail laid down by older males who already found a mate
They live in pairs from birth and travel together until they are old enough to spawn
context: In several anglerfish species the male is far smaller, bites onto a female, and fuses to her bloodstream — degenerating into a sperm-producing organ. The female may carry several fused males at once.

question: A clownfish colony in an anemone has one breeding female (the biggest), one breeding male, and several smaller fish waiting. If the female dies, something specific happens. What?
answer: The breeding male changes sex and becomes the new female, having been born able to do this
choices: The breeding male changes sex and becomes the new female, having been born able to do this
The largest waiting fish quickly grows to female size and takes over the breeding role
The colony abandons that anemone and merges with the nearest neighboring clownfish colony
All remaining fish remain male and the colony does not breed again that season at all
context: Clownfish are protandrous — born male, with the ability to become female. When the breeding female dies, the breeding male switches and the next-largest fish becomes the new breeding male. Sequential hermaphroditism is common in reef fish.

question: Cleaner wrasse and clownfish both change sex during life — but they switch in opposite directions. Cleaner wrasse are born female and become male. What controls the change in a wrasse colony?
answer: Dominance — when the dominant male dies, the largest female changes sex and takes his place
choices: Dominance — when the dominant male dies, the largest female changes sex and takes his place
Temperature — warm-season wrasse all switch together as a coordinated reef-wide event
Age — every wrasse becomes male at exactly the same age regardless of social rank or size
Diet — eating certain plankton species triggers the female-to-male transition in a wrasse
context: Cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus) are protogynous — born female, becoming male when social cues call for it. Sequential hermaphroditism in fish runs both ways depending on lineage. Wonder on its own biological terms.
